top_cited_works.title: Experimental investigation of a supersonic swept ramp injector using laser-induced iodine fluorescence
top_cited_works.abstract: Planar measurements of injectant mole fraction and temperature have been conducted in a nonreacting supersonic combustor configured with underexpanded injection in the base of a swept ramp. The temperature measurements were conducted with a Mach 2 test section inlet in streamwise planes perpendicular to the test section wall on which the ramp was mounted. Injection concentration measurements, conducted in cross flow planes with both Mach 2 and Mach 2.9 free stream conditions, dramatically illustrate the domination of the mixing process by streamwise vorticity generated by the ramp. These measurements, conducted using a nonintrusive optical technique (laser-induced iodine fluorescence), provide an accurate and extensive experimental data base for the validation of computation fluid dynamic codes for the calculation of highly three-dimensional supersonic combustor flow fields.

top_cited_works.abstract: Covers advancements in spacecraft and tactical and strategic missile systems, including subsystem design and application, mission design and analysis, materials and structures, developments in space sciences, space processing and manufacturing, space operations, and applications of space technologies to other fields.

top_cited_works.title: Aerodynamic Loads over Arbitrary Bodies by Method of Integrated Circulation
top_cited_works.abstract: A novel numerical method for the conversion of unstructured surface vorticity into directional integrated circulation has been presented. This method allows for the reduction of vorticity distributions on arbitrary three-dimensional bodies into their mathematically equivalent formulations in the Prandtl lifting-line theory. A discussion of its implementation into a practical numerical solver has been presented. This new solver was applied to simple wing shapes as well as complex aircraft geometries to demonstrate the applicability of such an approach to flow solvers. It was shown that the reduction to lifting-line theory was exact for simple shapes such as rectangular and elliptical wings. For complex aircraft geometries, such as leading-edge root extension and canard-equipped aircraft, it was shown that the method of integrated circulation allowed for accurate prediction of aircraft loads and the analysis of flow physics, in keeping with the Prandtl original concepts.

recent_works.title: Surrogate Modeling of Flight Behavior With Deep Neural Networks
recent_works.abstract: This paper explores the efficacy of generating aerodynamic data using a neural network as a surrogate model. We show that for the NASA N2A Hybrid Wing Body (HWB) aircraft and the NASA Generic T-tail (GTT) aircraft, we can generate highly accurate approximations of certain aerodynamic features, once that surrogate model has been trained on FlightStream® data. We suggest the use of a neural network surrogate model as a new approach for calculating approximate aerodynamic coefficients efficiently [ 5] and in a comparatively short time frame compared to vorticity solving software such as FlightStream® [2].

recent_works.title: Unsupervised Clustering of Solid Propellant Missile Systems Using Performance Parameters and Telemetry Data
recent_works.abstract: This paper describes the application of statistical learning techniques to unsupervised clustering of solid rocket motor-powered missile system designs. Two clustering scenarios are presented: one shows how to cluster missile data based on missile performance parameters, and the other shows how to use the "max" parameters of the trajectory for clustering. The first scenario reveals that missiles can easily be clustered using unsupervised training on well-partitioned data such as specific impulse and chamber pressure. This scenario will only utilize the raw data extracted from the missile, rather than the class of missiles from which the missile design was generated. This scenario, because it utilizes unsupervised learning, will also determine the number of clusters to use by only looking at the data extracted. The second scenario utilizes the max parameters of the flyout, such as apogee and downrange distance, to cluster the missile data in an unsupervised manner. Various clustering methods using different inputs are shown. recent_works.title: Analysis of a Generic T-Tail Transport Using a Surface-Vorticity Panel Method Flow Solver at Low Angles of Attack
recent_works.abstract: A panel method flow solver with viscous capabilities was used to determine stability characteristics, including dynamic stability derivatives, of a well-studied generic T-tail (GTT) transport aircraft model. Longitudinal, lateral, and directional static characteristics were computed using the steady and pseudo-steady state solver modes within the FlightStream panel method flow solver. The effects of control surface deflections were also investigated. Dynamic stability derivatives were computed using the pseudo-steady state and unsteady state solver modes. The results of each solver mode were compared in accuracy. The unsteady solver results were computed using the forced oscillation (F-O) method and post-processed using an integration method. All results were compared against published experimental and CFD data. Across all cases studied, the panel method results aligned well with wind tunnel data. Both solver modes used for dynamic derivative computations agree with published data in sign and relative magnitude. recent_works.title: Three-Dimensional Solid Rocket Motor Internal Ballistics With a Free-Vortex Method
recent_works.abstract: A novel method is developed to solve the internal flow field of solid rocket motors using free vortex elements. The goal of this work is to produce an efficient flow solver suitable for conceptual and preliminary design of solid rocket motors. The solid rocket motor is modeled as a paneled surface that represents the burning surface of the propellant in the combustion chamber. Vorticity is shed from the surface into vortex elements that flow freely through the internal domain. Results are provided for a cylindrical solid rocket motor, and the solution is compared with an analytical model. Good agreement is observed between the vortex method and the analytical solution. Internal flow solutions are obtained on the order of minutes.

recent_works.title: Improved prediction of propeller tonal noise through integration of Hanson's model into a modern surface-vorticity panel code
recent_works.abstract: This work aims at improving the precision of tonal noise prediction in urban air mobility (UAM) and general aviation applications, where noise reduction proves essential for vehicle certification and acceptance. To this end, classic acoustic theory is incorporated into a modern surface-vorticity panel code to predict the tonal noise of a benchmark propeller. Central to this research is Hanson's axially symmetric inflow formulation, an approach based on Goldstein's solution to Lighthill's wave equation. Throughout this effort, the accuracy and limitations of the resulting approach are validated using experimental data derived from NASA's Low Speed Aeroacoustic Wind Tunnel. The underlying evaluation enables us to confirm the model's reliability while establishing a basis to assess its efficacy when used in conjunction with a surface-vorticity solver. In this manner, the effective implementation of Hanson's axially symmetric inflow formulation within a modern surface-vorticity panel code is demonstrated.
